title: Flat stocks. A higher hurdle.
deck: My read on Thursday's completed session: a steady index does not mean financing pressure has eased. Jobless claims and Costco's results offer evidence of resilience, but resilience is not the same as a cheap valuation. Separate sustainable operating growth from price effects and one-off earnings benefits.

sections.title: The closing index hid a different bond-market message.
sections.body: AP recorded the S&P 500 at 7,704.13, down less than 0.1%; the Dow closed at 51,349.98 (−0.3%) and the Nasdaq Composite at 26,939.37, up less than 0.1%. Official Treasury par yields rose to 4.87% at two years, 5.18% at ten years and 5.47% at thirty years: increases of 2, 7 and 7 basis points. The 10Y–2Y spread widened from 26 to 31 basis points. My interpretation: the longer-term financing hurdle rose despite a nearly unchanged headline equity index. This does not prove investors ignored risk; improving earnings expectations could offset discount-rate pressure. Nor can nominal yields alone identify inflation compensation, real-rate changes or term premium.

sections.title: No claims surge—but do not confuse layoffs with hiring.
sections.body: The Labor Department reported 197,000 initial claims for the week ended 19 September, down 1,000 from a revised 198,000. The four-week average fell to 202,250. Continuing insured unemployment was 1,719,000 for the earlier week ended 12 September, up 2,000. All are seasonally adjusted. My assessment: these readings do not support an abrupt surge in benefit applications, which is a counterweight to a near-term demand-collapse narrative. But claims do not measure job creation, hours or wage purchasing power. The prior initial estimate was revised upward by more than the latest weekly decline, so the small headline change deserves less weight than a sustained trend.

sections.title: Costco grew, but not every headline percentage is underlying demand.
sections.body: Costco's 24 September release reported quarterly net sales of $93.9 billion, up 11.2%, for the 16 weeks ended 30 August. US comparable sales rose 10.7%, or 7.2% excluding gasoline-price and currency effects. Diluted EPS was $6.75, including a disclosed $0.15 non-recurring net benefit from tariff refunds. My inference: growth remains meaningful after the stated sales adjustments, but those adjustments do not remove all inflation or reveal unit volumes. Strong performance at one retailer could reflect market-share gains or value-seeking rather than uniformly healthy consumers. The release is company evidence, not an explanation of Thursday's index move.

sections.title: Normalize cash flows before changing the growth assumption.
sections.body: For a DCF, distinguish recurring operations from temporary benefits before setting the starting cash flow. Do not simply annualize a seasonal quarter or treat EPS as unlevered free cash flow. Then test a higher discount rate independently of sales growth. My preferred comparison is resilient operations with expensive capital versus weaker demand with margin pressure—not an automatic earnings downgrade because bond yields rose. A strong business can still require demanding assumptions to justify its valuation.

watch: Watch whether the claims trend changes across several releases and revisions, then compare with hiring and hours rather than drawing conclusions from a single weekly move.
Check company volumes, customer mix and cash conversion to distinguish real demand growth from price effects or market-share gains.
A sustained reversal in long-term yields without weaker operating evidence would soften the valuation headwind; continued increases would make cash-flow durability more important.
caveat: Codex's analysis, not Owen's personal view or investment advice. Market closes and Treasury observations cover 24 September, the latest completed US session at the displayed research cutoff. Research finished on 25 September, later than the scheduled morning run; this is not live commentary on that day's trading. Treasury figures are daily par yields, not executable market quotes. Claims refer to the distinct weeks stated and are subject to revision. Costco's release is dated 24 September and describes a quarter ended 30 August. Company evidence is not representative of every consumer or business. Interpretations are conditional; co-movement does not establish causation.
